title: Arp 286 (NGC 5560, 5566 & 5569)
caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 286 (NGC 5560, NGC 5566 and NGC 5569), imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
celestial: Arp 286, NGC 5560, NGC 5566, NGC 5569 · constellation Virgo
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Three gravitationally interacting galaxies make up Arp 286, in the constellation Virgo. The large spiral in the center is NGC 5566. Below it and to the left lies the small, blue spiral NGC 5569, and at the top is NGC 5560, a spiral that has been pulled out of shape.
NGC 5560's distortion is presumably caused by the gravity of NGC 5569. When galaxies pass close to one another, their mutual pull can warp and twist their discs.

Galaxies that are close neighbors can pull material out of each other, bend their arms and sometimes trigger new star formation. Groups of neighboring galaxies tugging on each other give astronomers a chance to watch, in a single snapshot, how gravity can reshape galaxies over time.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
